outline: 542 Summary Statistics from Tables and Graphs
767 Relative Frequency and the Law of Large Numbers

examples.question_text: A spinner is spun $75$ times and lands on Red $24$ times. Estimate the probability of Red as a fraction in simplest form and as a decimal.
examples.solution_text:
Use the observed frequency divided by the number of trials.
$\begin{aligned} P(\text{Red}) &\approx \frac{24}{75} \\ &= \frac{8}{25} \\ &= 0.32 \end{aligned}$

examples.question_text:
An experiment records these outcome frequencies.
$\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Outcome} & \text{Frequency} \\ \hline 14 & 17 \\ 15 & 11 \\ 16 & 23 \\ 17 & 19\end{array}$
Estimate the probability of outcome $16$, correct to $2$ decimal places.
examples.solution_text:
Add all frequencies to find the number of trials.
$\text{Total frequency} = 17+11+23+19 = 70$
$\begin{aligned} P(16) &\approx \frac{23}{70} \\ &= 0.328571\ldots \\ &\approx 0.33 \end{aligned}$
The estimated probability is $0.33$ to $2$ decimal places.

examples.question_text:
A four-sided spinner records the following scores.
$\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Score} & \text{Frequency} \\ \hline 1 & 9 \\ 2 & 14 \\ 3 & 18 \\ 4 & 9\end{array}$
Calculate the relative frequency of each score as a decimal.
examples.solution_text:
Each frequency is divided by the same total.
$\text{Total frequency} = 9+14+18+9 = 50$
$\begin{aligned} rf(1) &= \frac{9}{50} = 0.18 \\ rf(2) &= \frac{14}{50} = 0.28 \\ rf(3) &= \frac{18}{50} = 0.36 \\ rf(4) &= \frac{9}{50} = 0.18 \end{aligned}$
Check: $0.18+0.28+0.36+0.18=1$.

examples.question_text:
A simulation rolls a standard six-sided die using independent trials under stable conditions. The relative frequency of rolling a $6$ is recorded below.
$\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Number of rolls} & \text{Relative frequency of }6 \\ \hline 12 & 0.2500 \\ 200 & 0.1800 \\ 2000 & 0.1680 \\ 40000 & 0.1669\end{array}$
Explain how these results illustrate the Law of Large Numbers.
examples.solution_text:
The theoretical probability of rolling a $6$ is $\frac{1}{6}=0.1666\ldots$.
As the number of rolls increases, the recorded relative frequencies approach this probability. This illustrates the Law of Large Numbers; the relative frequency need not get closer after every trial.

examples.question_text:
Experiment A tosses a coin $20$ times. Experiment B tosses the same coin $800$ times. Both use comparable independent trials under stable conditions.
Which experiment generally gives a more reliable estimate of the probability of Heads? Explain how Experiment A could improve its estimate.
examples.solution_text:
Experiment B generally gives a more reliable estimate because its larger number of trials reduces typical random variation. It does not guarantee an estimate closer to the true probability.
Experiment A could toss the coin more times under comparable conditions, record the results and recalculate the relative frequency.

examples.derivation: 24/75 simplifies to 8/25 and equals 0.32. Dividing the observed frequency by the trial count follows source lines 770–783 and 899–904.
17+11+23+19=70. The selected outcome has relative frequency 23/70=0.328571…, giving an estimated probability of 0.33 to two decimal places. This follows the table method in source lines 787–810.
9+14+18+9=50. Dividing each frequency by 50 gives 0.18, 0.28, 0.36 and 0.18, which sum exactly to 1. This follows source lines 770–810 and 814–832.

The theoretical probability is 1/6=0.166666…. The displayed absolute differences are approximately 0.083333, 0.013333, 0.001333 and 0.000233. These results illustrate convergence towards the theoretical probability, consistent with the source investigation and explanation at lines 834–880. The solution correctly avoids promising improvement after every trial.

800 trials is 40 times the 20-trial sample. Under the stated comparable conditions, the larger sample generally reduces random variation. Increasing Experiment A's trial count, recording outcomes and recalculating relative frequency follows source lines 878–911; greater accuracy in an individual experiment is correctly not guaranteed.
